title: Leaving for Kansas City in 1929 and its stars
summary: He leaves Dallas for Kansas City, 1929-32, and lists the many musicians and club owners there.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Well, now we're coming to 1929. I decided after a while that the traveling fever...well, you know...was in my blood. It's pretty rugged to live in like the South, or some small town after you've experienced St. Louis and Washington and Louisville and all those towns, you know, and fast towns and you seen Ida Cox and Lovey Taylor and Trixie Smith and Mamie Smith and this...the feeling that I got of being somebody more important than just going over to some local dance hall and hear some guy play, hear somebody sing that are really amateurs. I just felt that I was above that. A show came to Dallas. I went to Tulsa; from Tulsa to Oklahoma City and from Oklahoma City to Kansas City. And I stayed in Kansas City from '29 to '32. And in 1932...this is in Kansas City when Count Basie was there and it meant nothing to see...[phone rings]
You were talking about when Count Basie was in Kansas City...

Well, we get to Kansas City...Kansas City to me at that point was the highlight. It wasn't the climax, but just the highlight...well, I don't guess it was the highlight, but it was such an exciting city, where that...at six o'clock you 'O have Julia Lee, George Lee, Andy Kirk, Mary Lou Williams, Hot Lips Page, Willie Mack Washington who was the first drummer with Bennie Moten, Jo Jones...well, I don't think Jo was around in the beginning. And then you'd have Dan Miner and Budd Johnson and Keg Johnson, Booker Pittman, Count Basie, Buster Moten, Buster Smith, Hot Lips Page, Walter Page, all of the musicians that...and Ben Webster...all of the musicians that you had known over the years and you had picked them as possibly going to the top of the heap, WERE in Kansas City. And then you had like Louis coming to town and you had Don Redman, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, you know, all of the leading attractions.

This was fascinating to me. And then I was...I called myself half-slick, you know what I mean. I was good friends with Ellis Burton, who was the owner of the Yellow Front Cafe, and Piney Brown...(unintelligible).. Piney Brown and--Big Piney had gone to Chicago to live, but Little Piney was there--and Felix Payne, who was another patron of jazz musicians. And Big Joe Turner, Jimmy Rushing. And this to me was just so fascinating and amazing, that I just couldn't...I couldn't really get it in my mind that here I am, Sammy Price, who the lady asked did I want to, you know, do
some work. And Sammy Price, who the music teacher said I would never play, I had no ideas. Flashbacks... [recording interruption]
